Building a brighter future for all We remain committed to helping the nation prosper and to improving living standards for all Australians. We have continued to support our customers and communities through changing economic conditions, while keeping the Bank safe and strong. As we look forward, we have refreshed our strategy to focus on supporting Australia’s economic growth – remaining at the centre of our customers’ financial lives, helping them access housing, grow and protect their wealth, and start, run and grow their business. Our purpose continues to inspire us to deliver for our customers and the nation. Significant judgements Each year we conduct a qualitative sustainability materiality assessment to identify and disclose against the sustainability-related topics most relevant to our stakeholders in our value chain and to the Bank. The assessment considers sustainability-related impacts, risks and opportunities that have the potential to influence CBA’s ability to create value over the short to medium term (1–5 years). This year’s assessment reviewed a range of sustainability topics, which were prioritised using our 5x5 risk matrix and exercised significant judgement. The prioritised topics were then grouped into overarching themes that informed the structure of this report. Theme selection involved significant judgement, guided by the results of our materiality assessment. Sustainability-related information includes non-financial information and refers to environmental, social and governance topics and themes that are important to our stakeholders and to CBA, as they have the potential to impact stakeholders and CBA’s financial prospects in the short to medium term. While some topics are traditionally linked to sustainability, others are included based on their perceived potential to materially impact our stakeholders and CBA’s financial prospects. We are committed to improving living standards for all Australians. By remaining a strong, safe and resilient bank, we can continue lending to our customers through economic cycles, investing for the future, and delivering sustainable returns for our shareholders. Rising geopolitical tensions, global economic challenges, and technological changes are causing many of our customers to feel financial pressure and uncertainty about their futures. Community concerns about housing and energy affordability, as well as intergenerational inequality, continue to grow. Australia’s economy remains resilient and relatively well positioned. Our country is still an attractive place to live, work and invest. We face headwinds which highlight the need for long-term economic reform and call for a confident vision for growth, fiscal responsibility with future generations in mind, and supply-side reform in areas like housing and energy. Australia also needs to maintain sovereignty of nationally important industries, including Australia’s financial system. Governments and industries need to work together to address challenging domestic issues and deliver a stronger future for Australia. Learn more about our operating context on pages 10–11. Refreshing our strategy We have made progress in our strategy to support customers through changing economic conditions. This year we lent $42 billion to businesses to help them grow and assisted over 140,000 households in buying a home. We have strengthened our focus on customer experience and consistently invested in leading technology and data capabilities. Importantly, we have continued to become a safer organisation with greater risk maturity, transparency and discipline. However, we know there is much more to do. invested in leading technology and data capabilities. Importantly, we have continued to become a safer organisation with greater risk maturity, transparency and discipline. However, we know there is much more to do. Our operating context has shifted, and we expect the next decade to bring complex geopolitical, reputational and competitive challenges. To better navigate the future, we have refreshed our strategy to continue positioning the Bank to deliver for our customers, communities, the nation and our shareholders. Our strategy considers diverse sustainability-related impacts, helping us address environmental, social, and governance risks and opportunities. We are making decisions today with a focus on long-term outcomes, even when they come at a short-term cost. We want to help build Australia’s future economy by supporting business growth and productivity. Productivity is key to improving living standards and its benefits need to be shared fairly so all communities can prosper. We are committed to allocating capital intentionally, ensuring banking services remain accessible, and advocating for a strong financial system and an economy that works for all Australians. Many Australians and Australian businesses trust us with their transaction banking and deposit relationship. We want to deliver experiences our customers value and continually deepen our relationships with them. Ongoing investment in leading technology, artificial intelligence (AI) and our people enables us to deliver personalised banking at scale. Our customers need banking to become simpler, safer and better. Improvements to our risk culture and risk management, combined with disciplined balance sheet and capital management, are essential to support the economy during crises and deliver good shareholder outcomes. Learn more about our strategic priorities on pages 16–25. Delivering for our customers Being the trusted financial partner for Australian retail and business customers remains key to our strategy and long-term success. We continue to support customers with a range of money management tools and educational materials. For customers facing financial difficulty, we have initiated more than 139,000 tailored payment arrangements. To serve a broad range of customers we are focused on delivering a better, safer and more efficient banking experience. Our purpose, building a brighter future for all, reflects our enduring commitment to Australia. It inspires us to be better for our customers, people and communities, and shows our optimism for the future. By maintaining our balance sheet strength and executing our strategy we can deliver on our purpose. MESSAGE FROM OUR CHAIR AND CEO We offer the largest branch and ATM network, Australia-based call centres and the nation’s most popular banking app. This year we extended our commitment to regional Australia, keeping all regional branches open until at least mid-2027, and converted 15 Western Australian Bankwest branches to be CBA-branded. During the year we have constructively participated in national policy discussions and advocated for changes that support safe, secure and reliable banking services. To keep pace with technological change, we invested $2.3 billion in modernising our systems, migrating data, and building world-class engineering and AI capabilities. To keep pace with technological change, we invested $2.3 billion in modernising our systems, migrating data, and building world-class engineering and AI capabilities. With persistently high levels of fraud, scams, cyber threats and financial crime, we have invested over $900 million this year to help protect our customers. We have also reduced customer fraud and scam losses by 76% since peak losses in late 2022. We continue to work with other organisations and Government to build national resilience against these threats which continue to impact too many customers. Learn more about our approach to sustainability on pages 68–99. Supporting a prosperous, resilient and optimistic nation A strong and resilient financial system is required to support a strong economy. Financial services play a vital role in our customers’ everyday lives. Disruptions and outages in banking services prevent customers from making payments or running their businesses. We also play an important role to support economic growth by lending to businesses. Maintaining strong capital and prudent balance sheet settings enables us to maintain necessary investment to deliver resilient and safe banking services, and support our customers and the economy. We carefully consider funding, credit and liquidity needs and monitor non-financial risks such as operational resilience, compliance with laws and regulations, and broader environmental and social risks. Australia needs a financial system that works for all stakeholders and inspires optimism about the future. We continue to share customer insights and other perspectives to help inform policies that can support a strong financial system and economy. Delivering sustainable performance Our financial results reflect our customer focus and disciplined execution of our strategic priorities. Our strong financial position enables us to continue supporting our customers and deliver a sustainable dividend. We have declared a final dividend of $2.60 per share, fully franked. Learn more about our financial performance on pages 26–33. Outlook We know many of our customers are still cautious with global volatility creating uncertainty. The Australian economy has remained resilient with strong fundamentals. Looking ahead, there are many reasons to feel optimistic about Australia’s future including modest economic growth, a healthy labour market and easing interest rates. Our role is to support our customers and the nation. We will stay focused on investing in our business and executing our strategy to bring our purpose to life. We will continue to work with key stakeholders to advocate for issues that are in the national interest, and policy settings that help sustainably support services that Australians value. Thank you On behalf of the Board and Executive Leadership Team, we would like to thank our people for their care and commitment to our customers, our customers for trusting us with their banking, and to you, our shareholders for your continued support. Macroeconomic and cost-of-living pressures Australia’s economy has continued to show resilience, supported by strong population growth along with healthy labour market conditions. While overall conditions remain strong, some household budgets, particularly for younger Australians, renters and mortgage holders, continue to face pressures from elevated interest rates, rising essential costs and housing affordability challenges. During the year inflation continued to ease within the Reserve Bank of Australia’s (RBA) target range allowing the RBA to start reducing official interest rates. While economic growth continues, rising public sector expenditure and low levels of productivity growth highlight the growing need for long-term economic reform. We maintain a conservative balance sheet, with capital, funding, and credit settings carefully managed to ensure resilience and ongoing support for our customers and the broader economy. Heightened geopolitical risks The global geopolitical environment continues to change with heightened tensions and policy uncertainty weighing on trade, energy and investment markets. Increasing global trade restrictions, strategic competition and regional conflicts are disrupting supply chains, limiting access to key technologies and reshaping capital flows. Cyber threats and attacks continue to evolve, requiring heightened vigilance by people and businesses. Australia’s banking system remains resilient. We actively assess downside scenarios through robust stress testing, scenario analysis, and balance sheet risk management to strengthen operational resilience and safeguard against potential shocks. The Bank is well positioned to navigate external challenges and continue supporting our customers and the broader economy. Evolving technology Advances in AI, data analytics and digital infrastructure are transforming the banking landscape. These technologies offer opportunities to enhance customer experience, streamline processes, and improve risk management and operational efficiency. At the same time, they introduce new risks – including cyber security threats, scams, privacy concerns and the use of AI. Rapidly adopting technology such as AI to modernise existing industries and build new industries is critical for our economy. Careful consideration will be needed to incentivise productive investment, build sovereign capability and retain economic benefits in Australia for all Australians. We continue to invest in modernising our technology platforms and strengthening cyber resilience to safeguard operations and provide secure, reliable services. We are committed to managing technology risks and engaging regulators to support safer and responsible innovation. Ongoing investment in technology, data, and our people is essential to maintaining trust, building long-term strength, and staying ahead of technology-led change. Competitive intensity Competition in the banking sector remains elevated, driven by rising customer expectations, digital innovation and industry participants pursuing greater market share. Customers are increasingly seeking personalised, high-value experiences and seamless service. Pricing pressure remains evident across deposits and lending, where customer demand for value and changing channel dynamics contribute to a highly competitive environment. As a bank, we are inherently exposed to reputational risk with issues such as data privacy, conduct and governance having the potential to quickly erode stakeholder confidence. Expectations continue to rise around transparency, the responsible use of data and AI, and the delivery of fairer and responsible outcomes. Stakeholders are also increasingly focused on how we support Australia’s economy and contribute to financial inclusion and broader community outcomes. The Bank has an important role to play. We are working closely with government and industry to support more sustainable outcomes for our customers and communities. These efforts are fundamental to maintaining financial system stability and resilience, and to supporting the long-term health of the Australian economy and society. Supporting our customers and communities The past few years have been challenging for Australian households and businesses, with higher inflation and cost-of-living pressures. We remain committed to supporting our customers, communities and the nation when they need us most. We maintained our focus on supporting customers with a range of options, which included improved access to hardship assistance and over 139,000 tailored payment arrangements for those most in need. More than three million customers each month use our digital money management tools to help them manage their finances. Keeping customers’ accounts safe and secure remains a priority. We invested more than $900 million this year to help protect our customers from fraud, scams, cyber threats and financial crime. Our continued investment helped reduce customer fraud and scam losses by over 30% this year. We acknowledge there is still more to be done. Our refreshed strategy elevates our focus on supporting the national agenda, prioritises investment in technology that provides customers with better, faster and safer banking, and invests in our people and branches to better serve our customers and communities. Financial system resilience, balance sheet strength and organic capital generation Global events and previous cycles have taught us the value of having funding flexibility, strong provisions, appropriate capital levels and balance sheet strength. Shocks are difficult to foresee but can drive up funding costs and result in a loss of confidence in financial institutions. Economic downturns put pressure on asset quality, profitability and capital. The resilience of the economy is linked to the resilience of our financial system. The Board fully supports management decisions that strengthen our balance sheet rather than temporarily maximise short-term earnings. History has also taught us that sustained profitability which generates organic capital underpins strong investor support for the sector. To sustainably deliver good outcomes for our customers, people and communities, we also need to generate shareholder returns. Our purpose and refreshed strategy focuses us on supporting Australia’s prosperity over the coming decade. With continuing global uncertainty, our long-term decision making and strong balance sheet positions CBA to support our customers and the nation. Australia has had a fortunate 30 years with our economy, living standards and wealth growing faster than most developed countries. More recently, a sustained increase in the cost of living and cost of running a business has weighed on Australian households and businesses. We have a collective responsibility to help Australia meet today’s challenges including housing affordability, improved living standards, inclusive growth and energy supply. The economy needs to remain fair, accessible, work for a broad range of stakeholders and support all Australians. It is essential for the next generation to feel optimistic that they can get ahead, have job prospects, buy a home, and start or grow a business. OUR APPROACH TO CORPORATE GOVERNANCE Generating returns above the cost of capital is a non-negotiable for banks to be able to support services for all Australians, the economy, invest in the future and deliver sustainable returns. We must remain vigilant in delivering safe and exceptional banking services efficiently. Learn more about our financial performance on pages 26–33. Managing our key risks Maintaining strong governance, having the right organisational culture and instilling accountability is essential for delivering good risk outcomes. The Board establishes the strategic objectives and risk appetite for the Bank. This is informed by the Risk & Compliance Committee and Audit Committee programs of work, as well as our operating environment. Our annual review of the Risk Management Declaration (RMD) saw us continue our focus on financial crime, cyber security and operational resilience. The Bank continues to have a well-developed approach to managing financial risks. We also remain focused on retaining the important progress we have made in managing non-financial risks while pursuing excellence in customer service. Overseeing non-financial risks continues to be a key focus for the Board. This includes understanding the steps being taken to protect the Bank and its customers from cyber security threats and financial crime. This year management walked the Board through a real-life disruption scenario to help us better understand the impacts to customers and the Bank to inform our risk tolerance and business continuity plans for critical operations. continuity plans for critical operations. Learn more about how we manage risk on pages 58–67. Executive oversight Your Board plays a key role in appointing the CEO and ensuring appropriate succession plans. Attracting, developing and retaining Executive talent with the right skills and values, at all levels, is needed to deliver our strategic ambition and enhance franchise value. The Board engages with the Executive Leadership Team (ELT) regularly. The People & Remuneration Committee reviews Executives’ performance through robust discussions to determine remuneration outcomes. It is not uncommon to hear from shareholders that they would like to see a performance and remuneration framework with greater weighting given to financial measures, to incentivise stronger alignment to shareholder returns. We agree with APRA that non-financial measures are important. We recognise the risk that a framework with more emphasis on earnings may bias management to make short-term decisions that are not in the long-term interests of shareholders, customers and the wider Australian economy. The Board has designed our framework to provide the right balance between delivering shareholder returns, customer outcomes and investing for the future. Our frameworks enable us to hold management to account and not overweight any one factor. Our long-term remuneration is designed to support a collective focus on generating sustainable long-term value and comply with requirements under APRA Prudential Standard CPS 511. Through the granting of equity instruments with long vesting periods, we reinforce the alignment of Executives’ experience with that of our shareholders. For example, when shareholder returns are less favourable, Executives share the impact in lower vesting outcomes and a reduction in the value of their long-term holdings, although we acknowledge the outcome for Executives can still be positive. Learn more about our approach to remuneration on pages 182–218. Having a balanced mix of skills, experience and perspectives to address current and emerging risks and opportunities, and facilitating robust discussions remains a key focus. Our skills matrix is regularly reviewed. To get the long-term settings right, the Board requires deep banking; strategy; technology; regulation and risk; customer; operational expertise running large businesses; and financial decision-making experience. The Board oversees the Bank’s corporate governance framework. The Board has established four standing Committees to assist it in carrying out its functions. Board Committee roles and responsibilities are detailed in their respective charters. Our Board in action Board planning and agenda setting This year the Board held 12 meetings, including six multi-day Board and Committee meetings with structured agendas, six shorter Board meetings and two strategy deep dives, which were held as part of the multi-day Board meetings. Certain CBA Directors also met with non-executive directors of Commonwealth Bank of Australia (Europe) N.V. and ASB, as well as senior executives of CBA India. There is also engagement between Committee Chairs and their equivalent at Commonwealth Securities Limited (CommSec). So that the Board and Committees’ time is used efficiently, and discussions reflect the Bank’s priorities, agendas are reviewed by the respective Chairs, in consultation with the Group Company Secretary and the CEO. Forward planners help provide a comprehensive view of upcoming agendas, allowing for adjustments as priorities evolve. The Board retains flexibility for ad hoc matters to be discussed at meetings where appropriate. Effective communication between management and the Board ahead of Board and Committee meetings is facilitated through management input into certain agenda items and attending pre-meetings with Committee Chairs and the Group Company Secretary. and the Board ahead of Board and Committee meetings is facilitated through management input into certain agenda items and attending pre-meetings with Committee Chairs and the Group Company Secretary. To promote effective decision making and a consistent approach to writing papers, Board and Committee paper templates are available and training on writing papers is offered to preparers, throughout the year. Overseeing the delivery of our strategy Our governance practices play an essential role in providing oversight of the Bank’s operations and contribute to the development of our strategy. The Board is responsible for endorsing strategic and business unit plans to be implemented by management. This includes approving financial plans, which incorporate strategic and other perspectives. The Board oversees the strategy through Board meetings and strategy deep dives. Oversight of material sustainability-related risks and opportunities The Board receives management reports on sustainability-related topics. For example, this year the Board approved the diversity, equity and inclusion 2025–2028 strategy, including our gender equity action plan. The Board also considers the environmental and social (E&S) impact of the Bank’s activities and oversees management of climate risk, within the Bank’s overall business strategy and risk appetite. The Board holds the CEO and ELT accountable for delivering their E&S responsibilities. For example, ahead of review by the Board, the Financial Risk Committee reviewed the results of the annual climate risk materiality assessment. Board meetings The CEO and Executives provide regular reports to the Board. In this way, the Board receives an update on the Group’s performance and the performance of each Executive’s business or support unit. Progress against strategy is a key component of these reports. Standalone agenda items relating to strategic matters are also discussed at each multi-day Board meeting. The topics discussed throughout the year include the Business Plan and reports on customers, business performance, operating environment, acquisitions, technology strategy and environmental strategy. The Board and Committee Chairs are responsible for fostering open, inclusive, and where appropriate, robust discussion and debate. Strategy deep dives The Board held two strategy deep dives this year. These were opportunities for the Board to reflect on the strategy, consider the evolving external environment, review progress against the Bank’s priorities and identify opportunities to do more. This included breakout topic sessions for the Board, as well as input from external subject matter experts. In December, the Directors considered the Bank’s historical and future operating context to inform our refreshed strategy. The refreshed strategy, how we will measure success, key enablers and execution priorities for next year were discussed at the April strategy deep dive. Our Risk Management Framework (RMF) outlines the Bank’s expectations on how we identify, measure, monitor and respond to our risks. Our RMF is comprised of systems, structures, policies, processes and people. They work together to help identify, assess and mitigate our internal and external sources of risk. We categorise the material risks the Bank is exposed to as strategic, financial and non-financial risks. Each material risk type has its own specific framework or requirements to manage the risk. These material risks and our approach to managing them are set out in our RMF. The RMF is reviewed annually by the ELT and the Board. The RMF is also independently reviewed every three years by an external reviewer, supported by internal and external audit programs. These reviews of the RMF as well as our annual RMD to APRA, set out our plans to strengthen the RMF in support of our strategy. The RMF enablers facilitate the effective identification, measurement, monitoring and response to our material risks. They help us translate the RAS into our daily business activities. Risk governance and reporting The Board has ultimate responsibility for the Bank’s risk governance, including the RMF and its implementation by management. The Board is supported by its four Committees as well as management-level committees that oversee our material risks. Management regularly provides information to the Board which allows material risk positions to be monitored against the RAS and policy limits. Risk accountabilities and skills The Three Lines of Accountability model (3LoA) organises our accountabilities to manage the Bank’s risks by separating the roles. Line 1 own and manage the risks whereas Line 2 develop risk frameworks and provide assurance. Line 3 provide independent assurance over how effectively risks are being managed. The 3LoA include skilled employees within each line and are supported by risk capabilities, and performance and remuneration frameworks. Our remuneration framework supports accountability by incorporating risk assessment as gate openers and modifiers in employee and executive remuneration. How we make decisions Risk appetite The RAS is reviewed and approved annually by the Board in line with our operating context, and is adapted for new and changing risks present in our operations. The Board-approved RAS helps embed a culture focused on disciplined risk management to enable smart risk taking. The RAS also includes key risk indicators for our material risks. This provides signals for building levels of risk and encourages management to take action and avoid a breach of appetite. In addition to governance of RAS performance through Board and management-level committees, our Group policies, procedures, delegations and limits translate and embed the RAS into our daily business activities. Risk culture Our risk culture reflects our beliefs and behaviours within the Bank and determines how we identify, measure, monitor and respond to risks. These behaviours guide decision making and good risk management, and embody our values and leadership principles. This helps our actions align to our core beliefs. To sustain and improve our risk culture, senior management and the Board form a view of the Bank’s risk culture through an annual Board risk culture assessment. This is supported by the Group risk culture response plan, which addresses areas of focus identified by the Board. It is further reinforced by self-reflections on business unit risk culture to drive improvement at the team level. Risk measurement We use multiple techniques to identify and measure risks the Bank is exposed to. These include stress testing and scenario analysis; risk and control self-assessments; compliance self-assessments; emerging risk assessment; systems and models to quantify risks and identify risk exceptions; assurance of the RMF in the form of Line 1 controls testing; Line 2 assurance reviews and framework approvals; Line 3 internal audits; and the external audit program. Stress testing Stress testing and scenario analysis are important risk management tools. They enable the Board and senior management to better understand, quantify and manage risks. They also inform how we may respond to risk events occurring and any potential weaknesses in our actions during a crisis. The results of these stress tests are important for strengthening our risk management approach. Stress testing results also inform our risk appetite and assist us in identifying the acceptable levels of risk we will assume in our operations. Manage and control risks We implement measures to manage and control risks within appetite such as: detective and preventative controls; limits; delegated authorities and review and approval processes; policies and procedures; and issue and incident management. # Board Risk & Compliance Committee Board Risk & Compliance Committee The Board Risk & Compliance Committee reviews and oversees the RMF and adherence to the Bank’s Board-approved risk appetite. The Committee monitors our risk profile against changes in our operating context. Management provides regular reports to the Committee to provide oversight of current and emerging risks, the effectiveness of our control environment and our risk management practices. It is important for directors to spend the right amount of time on the right issues. This year the Committee’s focus remained on the management of financial risks such as funding and liquidity, and non-financial and strategic risks, including cyber security, fraud and scams, operational resilience, privacy, data, environmental and social, artificial intelligence and financial crime compliance. The Risk & Compliance Committee meets six times per year, or more frequently if needed, with the Chair of the Committee reporting to the Board after each Committee meeting. The Committee also supports the Board’s concurrent meetings. It provides updates on relevant risk outcomes and matters at the concurrent meetings to support the assessment of remuneration outcomes for the CEO and Group Executives and performance outcomes of the Group Auditor. Emerging risks are often driven by new trends in our operating environment, such as competition, new technologies, regulation or evolving customer expectations. We continue to invest in detection and case management capabilities to better assess risk across customers, channels and products, while strengthening our AML/CTF compliance to meet regulatory obligations in Australia and other jurisdictions. To support identification and management of risk, we systematically review guidance from regulators, intergovernmental bodies such as the Financial Action Task Force, and non-government resources to understand and address emerging financial crime trends and typologies. Chair and CEO Meeting Australia’s 2030 interim emissions reduction target requires significant investment. Estimates suggest Australia’s transition to net zero needs more than $600 billion of investment by 2050 to decarbonise the nation’s industry and energy systems. CBA can support our customers to fund their transition. The energy sector continues to be the biggest contributor to Australia’s domestic emissions. We believe that affordably decarbonising Australia’s electricity grid remains the most important step for Australia. Australia’s future economy needs more affordable and reliable energy Historically, Australia has been a reliable energy producer and exporter, making affordable energy prices a competitive advantage. As we transition to a net zero economy, we need to maintain this advantage to support Australian living standards and help build a brighter future for all. The demand for electricity in Australia is increasing due to economic and population growth, increased digitisation and electrification. Access to affordable and reliable energy sources is needed to support Australia’s prosperity and future economy. While progress on meeting Australia’s renewable energy target is commendable, over reliance on one energy source can lead to vulnerabilities in our electricity markets, blackouts and increased costs, putting more pressure on energy bills. We welcome the Australian Energy Market Operator’s (AEMO) work on approaches to grid stability. All energy sources and grid stability approaches have trade-offs such as emissions intensity, cost, time-to build and impacts on nature. We see an important role for governments and industries to balance and communicate those trade-offs and develop sound policies. Building community support for Australia’s transition to net zero is important. We welcome policies that can help Australia deliver more affordable and reliable energy for all Australians, now and into the future. Balancing trade-offs to support the transition Australia needs effective climate change policies that reduce emissions, provide investment certainty, support economic growth, and minimise increased costs for essential goods such as food and electricity. Energy security is crucial to the success of the Australian economy. Australia is facing a critical moment in the energy transition, needing to deliver important national energy infrastructure that lowers emissions quickly and affordably. Limiting global warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels appears increasingly difficult and the pathway to net zero, globally, is looking narrower. The Australian Government is continuing to develop a national Net Zero Plan to guide our country’s transition to meet our legislated target of net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. Australia’s transition to a net zero economy by 2050 is underway. Government policies, and new generation and transmission infrastructure are assisting. As the bank for all Australians, we remain committed to helping our customers and supporting Australia’s transition to net zero by 2050. Our goals and targets remain aligned to 1.5°C scenarios. We believe this continues to be the right setting against which to track our progress. Expanding renewables in Australia’s electricity grid has been challenging due to insufficient transmission infrastructure and complex planning processes across different levels of government. AEMO has modelled that Australia can meet its renewable target provided planned investments are delivered, making critical energy infrastructure a national priority. Policy coordination is also needed to better integrate consumer energy resources into the grid, benefitting the system and all consumers. Grid reliability risks include extreme weather, energy shortfalls and operational issues with ageing coal-fired power generators facing early closure. Government and national energy bodies have signalled gas will remain a key part of Australia’s energy mix during the transition. This is a pragmatic trade-off, as gas currently remains critical for key industrial processes, as well as serving as a secure and reliable back-up to renewables. Continuing to support our customers Given one in three Australians and one in four Australian businesses call us their main financial institution, we play an important role in financing economic activity. However, the main driver of emissions reductions for our retail and small business customers is Australia’s electricity grid transitioning. We continue to provide lending products and tools that can help our customers understand the actions they can take to reduce their emissions, make their homes and businesses more energy efficient and aim to ease cost-of-living pressures. Harder-to-abate sectors, such as transport, agriculture and heavy industry are important sectors for Australia’s future economy and need balanced, long-term support to transition. While these sectors make up a smaller portion of our lending, compared to housing, our aim is to continue working with our customers in these sectors and exploring ways we can help them reduce their environmental impact. The Bank’s exposure to the upstream oil and gas extraction sectors is low at <0.1% of total committed exposures (TCE). Our lending portfolio will continue to evolve alongside Australia’s energy transition. Our Environmental and Social (E&S) Policy and Framework has long recognised Australia’s need for a secure energy platform. We expect certain upstream oil and gas extraction and coal-fired power generation customers to have Transition Plans, including Scope 3 emissions, before we provide corporate or trade finance, or bond facilitation. This year we reviewed the settings in our E&S Policy and Framework. Following our review, we are expanding our Transition Plan requirements to include thermal coal clients who derive 25% or more of their revenue from the sale of thermal coal. Our policy settings continue to reinforce our climate strategy. Looking ahead Physical climate risks to homes, national infrastructure and communities pose a growing challenge for affordability, insurability and long-term economic resilience. With only around 20% of Australia’s $60 billion nationally significant infrastructure initiatives designed to mitigate climate risks, there is more work to do on building national climate resilience. We would welcome reforms that build a shared understanding of physical climate risks to help inform decisions by households, lenders, insurers and governments. With appropriate sharing of costs and benefits, we believe Australia can transition to net zero by 2050 and create a brighter future for all. # Supporting Supporting Australia’s energy transition As Australia’s economy and population grows, households and businesses electrify, and digitisation increases, the demand for electricity will continue to grow. A reliable and affordable electricity grid is integral to the economy and Australia’s future prosperity. Electricity accounts for around 34% of Australia’s emissions. Decarbonising the electricity grid is critical to the decarbonisation of other sectors, including housing – the largest sector that CBA finances. For Australia, and the Bank, to achieve its emissions reduction ambitions, the electricity grid needs to decarbonise. Replacing coal-fired power stations with renewables is challenging. The nation needs to address long planning timeframes, supply chain constraints and increase community support for infrastructure. Installing rooftop solar remains popular with consumers. The Government’s renewable energy target provided Australia with direction. Recent policies including the Capacity Investment Scheme and Rewiring the Nation are helping to accelerate the transition. With generation capacity and transmission infrastructure progressing, Australia is better placed to meet its 2030 target of a 43% reduction in emissions below 2005 levels. It is our understanding that Australia should be able to produce sufficient generation to meet growing demand over the next decade, provided current State and Federal Government projects to build renewable and dispatchable generation, transmission assets and policies to coordinate consumer energy resources eventuate. Ongoing monitoring, policy adjustments and managing new challenges are essential for helping Australia remain on track. Achieving Australia’s emissions targets and producing reliable, affordable energy requires effective community engagement and policies that seek to maintain our country’s energy advantage. Affordably decarbonising Australia’s electricity grid is essential for Australia’s economy. CLIMATE DISCLOSURES Reducing emissions in key sectors Australia’s Climate Change Authority (CCA) has published six sector pathways. 1 The CCA’s report identifies potential technologies and actions for each sector that, taken together, could deliver net zero emissions for Australia by 2050. Given the significant progress in executing our reduction strategies for Scope 1 and 2, we are increasing our reduction target from 42% to 75% by 2030 against our 2020 baseline. the significant progress in executing our reduction strategies for Scope 1 and 2, we are increasing our reduction target from 42% to 75% by 2030 against our 2020 baseline. We are also able to expand our Scope 1 and 2 target coverage from 2026 onwards as we now have better data for our other overseas offices, including India. We have also made several changes to improve how we measure, manage and represent Scope 3 operational emission sources, particularly those associated with our supply chain. Where we do not currently have activity data available, we are developing spend-based estimates. We have conservatively estimated our expanded footprint as an increase of approximately 600% from our reported 2024 operational emissions. As our current Scope 3 target accounts for only 13% of our expanded estimated emissions, the existing Scope 3 target is no longer meaningful in its present form. Accordingly, we will reassess this target and focus on more accurately quantifying our Scope 3 operational emissions in line with new mandatory climate reporting requirements in 2026. Supporting action outside our operations We do not use carbon credits to meet our operational emissions targets. However, we continue to support climate action beyond our value chain, such as purchasing carbon credits and investing to help reduce our travel emissions. This year CBA signed several multi-year agreements supporting improved social, cultural and environmental impacts through projects within the ACCU scheme. Our portfolio focuses on projects supporting Australia’s Indigenous communities and aligns with our Reconciliation Action Plan. This year CBA supported Indigenous savanna burning projects which also have benefits for nature. Selected projects went through a due diligence assessment, to assess the integrity and credibility of the carbon credits generated. This due diligence assessment was based on the Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market’s Core Carbon Principles and transparency changes to the ACCU scheme. We continue to monitor developments related to the ACCU scheme and note the review Climate Active is currently undertaking. We will reassess our position as more information becomes available. In 2024, ASB pre-purchased carbon credits for 2025 sourced from GHG removal projects under the Permanent Forest Sink Initiative (PFSI). In 2024, Toitū Envirocare announced its commitment to align their practices with international standards. As a result, they will be moving towards no longer accepting carbon credits issued under the New Zealand PFSI for offsetting purposes. Toitū Envirocare honours the use of pre-purchased, ‘reserved’ New Zealand credits. As part of the transition phase, ASB will apply 2024 pre-purchased credits sourced from New Zealand-based PFSI compliant projects to maintain its Toitū Envirocare Net Carbon Zero certification. We also continue to take steps to reduce the impact of our office and branch fit-outs by making them more resource efficient. Our refurbishment projects incorporate sustainable design principles, and we look to reuse and repurpose existing building materials and furniture, wherever possible. A circular design approach is being taken, facilitating efficient installation and easy disassembly for repairs and reuse. In addition, our latest container branch, designed to support communities after natural disasters, considers sustainable design principles. The container itself has been reused, and approximately 70% of its interior is fitted with lower-carbon and circular materials, such as wall linings made from upcycled packaging, recycled plastic acoustic panelling and furniture, as well as lower-carbon carpet and joinery panels. COMMONWEALTH BANK 2025 ANNUAL REPORT CREATING VALUE SUSTAINABILITY FINANCIAL REPORT CLIMATE DISCLOSURES DIRECTORS’ REPORT ADDITIONAL INFORMATION OVERVIEW ESG Credit Standard We have explicitly incorporated the consideration of ESG risk assessments into our credit risk framework through our ESG Credit Standard. The standard provides a structured framework for the way in which E&S risks are to be considered in credit risk assessment processes for our customers. Along with all our other group-wide credit standards, it establishes the minimum credit expectations and requirements for identifying, managing and monitoring a borrower or counterparty’s E&S risks. The standard, which is applicable across the Bank, requires that existing or new non-retail borrowers or counterparties that meet certain criteria be considered against the commitments in the Bank’s E&S Framework when performing a credit assessment. Throughout the credit process, E&S risks identified are assessed for their impact on our customers’ ability to repay. In some cases, the standard also requires reviewing the borrower’s collateral they pledge to the Bank for E&S risks. We have not currently identified a globally accepted, standardised methodology for quantifying climate-related impacts on credit risk. Therefore, our ESG credit assessments continue to be driven by customer due diligence and qualitative assessments in processes tailored to the risk of specific portfolios. We expect our approach to integrating ESG into our credit risk framework will continue to evolve and adapt as industry practices mature, and as regulatory and stakeholder expectations change. Risk appetite statement The Board-approved RAS defines the maximum risk allowable to deliver the Bank’s strategic priorities. Management is required to operate within risk appetite. We have integrated two quantitative RAS indicators to help minimise potential credit losses from portfolios with higher exposure to climate-related risks. These focus on physical risk in the retail portfolio and transition risk in the institutional portfolio. We aim to use scenarios that: • are considered credible global climate scenarios • have plausible and appropriately severe outcomes • are consistent with market practices • support comparability with other organisations by using consistent input variables. Our long-term climate scenarios are based on the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) scenarios. This is a set of scenarios, developed by an international network of central banks and supervisors, to provide a common and up-to-date reference point for exploring how climate change, climate policy and technological trends could unfold under different futures. The NGFS scenarios incorporate the latest climate science findings, recent economic and climate data, country-level policy commitments to reach net zero emissions, and the latest trends in renewable energy and mitigation technologies. We prioritise our scenario analysis work based on the size of our lending portfolios, their exposure to climate-related risks and our ability to conduct analyses based on the availability of data. They explore futures with high transition risk (net zero 2050), higher transition risk (delayed transition) and higher physical risk (current policies). These three NGFS scenarios were selected to enable the assessment of a range of plausible climate physical and transition risk outcomes. To date, global progress against the goals of the Paris Agreement has lagged, increasing risk of the net zero 2050 scenario being out of reach. The delayed transition and current policies scenarios were selected as the Bank believes slower global progress in climate policy increases the probability of either scenario occurring. The NGFS scenario macroeconomic forecasts were tailored to the Australian context by an external economic advisory firm (Oxford Economics), and then modelled using the Bank’s suite of stress testing models to determine balance sheet and credit loss results extending out to 2050. The purpose of these NGFS-aligned scenarios is to identify impact trends that climate change could have over time on the broader economy, certain industry sectors and ultimately the Bank. The scenarios do not attempt to predict the timing and severity of individual acute physical or abrupt transition events that could impact the Bank’s financial performance in any given year. Rather, the cumulative effects of such events are factored into macroeconomic variables used to model these trends. Although this approach enables a clearer view of any trends over time, it likely underestimates potential losses to the Bank because it does not account for localised declines, or direct impacts on, asset values from severe climate physical or transition events that could occur in any given year. Therefore, three acute, event-driven scenarios were conducted to supplement this view (see pages 152–153). CLIMATE DISCLOSURES Why we ran this scenario Droughts have been a feature of the Australian landscape throughout history and can have severe impacts on the environment, industries, economy and people. Climate change is increasing temperatures and affecting rainfall, evaporation and climate systems in Australia, with climate projections indicating that droughts may be more severe and last longer. We ran this scenario to enhance our understanding of the potential losses to the Bank should a long-term drought lead to a substantial decline in farm values. Key scenario assumptions The scenario assumes a severe drought lasting for 10 years across parts of the Murray-Darling Basin and Western Australia. The scenario assumes farm values decline in the high-drought impact areas, the drought occurs during a high interest rate environment for reasons unrelated to the drought and the effectiveness of government support declines over the scenario. Insights from our analysis Total losses to the Bank over the 10 years are assessed to be below $500 million, split relatively evenly between farming – mainly grain growing, mixed farming and beef cattle farming – and agriculture adjacent industries, mainly from food manufacturing and farm produce wholesaling. Why we ran this scenario AEMO noted in the 2024 ISP that 90% of Australia’s coalfired power generators are forecast to retire by 2035, and are becoming less reliable and more difficult to maintain. Investment is needed urgently and new generation, storage and firming must be in place before coal-fired power stations retire. We ran this scenario to enhance our understanding of the potential losses to the Bank from a long-term electricity outage caused by two coal-fired power stations becoming simultaneously inoperable. The CRMA assesses how current and anticipated climate-related risks and opportunities arising from each of the futures outlined in our long-term scenarios, may impact the Bank’s material risk types, strategy, business model and value chain across the current, short, medium and long term. The assessment of impacts to our material non-financial and strategic risk types was performed through workshops with senior management and risk type owners, including ASB. The assessment of financial risk impacts incorporated outcomes from both the long-term and acute scenarios performed this year: • The long-term scenarios provided a perspective on impact trends that climate change could have over time on the broader economy, certain industry sectors and the Bank. • The acute event scenarios enabled us to assess the ability of the Bank to withstand severe, yet plausible, events that could occur in any given year under these futures. The anticipated effects on the Bank under these scenarios were considered across four time horizons: • Current term (within the next 12 months). • Short term (~3 years) to align with the Bank’s strategic planning cycle. • Medium term (~10 years) to align with the timeframe of when physical impacts begin to diverge for the low versus high warming futures. • Long term (~30 years) to align with the Bank’s home loan portfolio where home loans can be contractually agreed to for up to 30 years. The risk ratings indicate the impact

align with the timeframe of when physical impacts begin to diverge for the low versus high warming futures. • Long term (~30 years) to align with the Bank’s home loan portfolio where home loans can be contractually agreed to for up to 30 years. The risk ratings indicate the impact of climate change on the relevant risk type under each scenario. For financial risks and capital adequacy risk, ratings were determined with reference to the relevant Board approved RAS. For non-financial, E&S and AI risks our 5x5 risk matrix was applied. Risk appetite statement – Risk ratings were set based on the expected position relative to the relevant Board approved RAS thresholds. For example, a financial impact resulting in the Bank being outside risk appetite would be rated as ‘very high risk’. 5x5 risk matrix – Our risk matrix, updated in 2025, considers the impact and expected frequency of a risk eventuating, resulting in risks being rated as either low, moderate, medium, high or very high risk. Impact and frequency are assessed using the following: • Expected frequency ranges from ‘1 event every 10 years’ to ‘Multiple events in the next year’; and • Impacts uses a combination of qualitative factors and financial measures. Qualitative factors consider impacts on customers, our operations and people, shareholders, communities, and regulatory and legal. The quantitative financial impacts range from negligible ≤$1 million; minor >$1 million; major >$5 million; significant >$25 million; or critical >$100 million. For example, a medium risk rating could arise from an event expected to occur once every 10 years, with a significant financial impact of $25 million to $100 million. Alternatively, a medium risk rating could also arise from multiple events expected to occur in the next year, but with a minor impact of $1 million to $5 million. Each risk was assessed based on its impact to the Bank in the time horizon in which the relevant scenario occurs, rather than cumulative impacts over all time horizons. When assessing impacts for future time horizons under these scenarios, no additional material changes to the business model or control environment were assumed beyond those already in place. For example, while a potential strategic shift could mitigate some risks in the future, such changes were not factored into the future risk ratings. We acknowledge that available data and techniques to perform this type of assessment are still maturing across the industry. As a result, our assessment of the impacts of climate-related risks involves a greater reliance on assumptions than is typically required for more mature risk types, where historical data is a better predictor of future events. As data and assessment techniques improve over time, we anticipate that our future CRMAs will incorporate more advanced assessment techniques. For information on our long-term and acute scenarios, see pages 150–151 and 152–153, respectively. Climate-related effects can be widespread and interrelated, and may influence our operations, strategy and financial outcomes over the short, medium and long term. As per the result of our CRMA, no climate-related risks or opportunities were noted this year that have had a material impact on the Bank’s financial performance, financial position or cash flows. Anticipated impacts on our financial statements In some years, the Bank may experience increases in credit losses due to extreme weather events, however the scenario results indicate that financial impacts to the Bank from climate-related impacts are not expected to be material. This reflects the nature of our operations, the sectors in which we operate, and our existing risk management frameworks and portfolio diversification, which together provide a degree of resilience against potential climate-related impacts. The Bank is well placed to identify and pursue available opportunities arising from Australia’s transition to net zero by 2050. For example, the development of sustainable finance products, tools and services to support customers to transition and adapt to the impacts of climate change. While climate change presents challenges to the Australian economy and our communities, our core business remains resilient. A relatively small proportion of the Group’s TCE is currently exposed to high or very high physical or transition risk. Our customers have historically demonstrated strong repayment performance and we have established support mechanisms to assist them in times of financial stress, including those potentially arising from climate-related events. Although severe climate-related events could result in an increase in single year credit losses, these losses are assessed as a medium risk to the Bank as they would not result in a breach of our current capital, liquidity or profitability RAS indicators. This reflects our strong provisioning levels and capital position. For further details on our credit risk, see Note 9.2 on page 311 in the Financial report. CLIMATE DISCLOSURES Other climate-related risk assessment tools Supplier risk governance tool In June 2023 we introduced the environmental risk assessment in the supplier risk governance (SRG) tool. As part of CBA’s annual review, industry environmental risk ratings are updated to support the inherent environmental risk assessment of our suppliers. For suppliers in industries with high risk ratings, assessments are undertaken when onboarding for new services, or variation or renewal of an existing service, and form part of supplier risk screening before contracts are executed. For suppliers in industries with high risk ratings, assessments are undertaken when onboarding for new services, or variation or renewal of an existing service, and form part of supplier risk screening before contracts are executed. In 2024, in addition to the assessments that were completed when onboarding suppliers in high-risk industries, we triggered the environmental risk assessment for our leasing agents and landlords, and our top 100 suppliers by spend. As a result, the number of suppliers assessed decreased from last year and now totals 71. Of these suppliers, all reported they had no regulatory environmental breaches over the past three years. Climate stress index for agriculture In May 2024, we launched the climate stress index (CSI) tool for our bankers, developed in collaboration with CSIRO. The CSI tool forecasts climate stress through to 2030 by postcode, based on key agri-climatic productivity variables across grain, livestock and dairy sectors. It provides a composite score for each postcode-commodity combination indicating whether climate stress is expected to decrease, remain stable, or increase moderately or at a high rate. The tool enhances our understanding of the degree, nature and location of chronic climate risks to our lending securities. Currently, 19% of the Bank’s relevant agricultural exposures are secured by properties located in postcodes with forecasted increasing rates of climate stress. The tool enables our bankers to have conversations with customers on their long-term climate adaptation plans relevant for credit risk assessment. CSI insights are also used for portfolio monitoring in livestock, grain and dairy commodities, helping us track exposure trends and inform strategic planning. Insights from the tool can be shared with customers through a Climate Insight Report, tailored to their region and commodities, to help them consider the data and plan for future climate-related resilience. We will retire our productivity mapping tool given the launch of the CSI which provides a forward view of climate risk. DISCLOSURES Capital deployment Capital deployment relating to climate-related risks and opportunities may be categorised into the following: Financing: Climate-related financing refers to the offering of lending products, credit facilities, or other financing solutions that support customers in addressing their climate-related risks or pursuing their climate-related opportunities. Our SFT monitors the level of cumulative funding within the scope of our SFT eligibility criteria. Investment: Climate-related investment refers to capital deployed through financial instruments or equity stakes in public or private markets that relate to the Bank’s climate-related risks or opportunities and where climate considerations form a material part of the investment rationale or potential outcomes. This year CBA invested $46 million in climate-related investments. Expenditure: Climate-related expenditure refers to capital or operational spending incurred in managing climate-related risks or pursuing climate-related opportunities. This includes direct costs related to internal systems, infrastructure, tools or processes that are focused on climate risk mitigation, adaptation or resilience. No material direct climate-related expenditure was noted this year. Indirect costs include ongoing expenditure which would be incurred ordinarily, making it impractical to allocate costs as specifically climate-related. These indirect costs include activities such as branch and office refurbishments where we are actively incorporating sustainable practices through branch design and energy efficient retrofits; the ATM refresh project which incorporates lower carbon, natural and renewable materials; and the resourcing costs associated with ESG teams who work to deliver our climate strategy. For more information on our SFT, see page 172. Internal carbon price The Bank does not currently apply or use an internal carbon price. # Dear Shareholder Dear Shareholder Our 2025 financial year remuneration outcomes reflect consistent, disciplined execution of our strategic priorities, strong progress on initiatives to safeguard our customers and community, and sustainable returns for our shareholders. Remuneration report I am pleased to present the 2025 remuneration report. As a Board we oversee the Bank’s remuneration framework, regularly reviewing its policies and practices for effectiveness and alignment with our principles. It is pleasing that during the year, an independent review was completed to fulfil the requirements of the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority (APRA) Prudential Standard CPS 511 (CPS 511). The review found our framework is effective, supports the Bank’s culture and strategy and is aligned to positive risk outcomes, long-term soundness, and sustainable performance. Additionally, this year the People & Remuneration Committee completed a comprehensive review of our executive remuneration framework in the context of emerging Australian and global market trends in executive remuneration. Our assessment is that the framework remains fit for purpose, aligned to shareholder value creation, and compliant with regulatory requirements. Following the review, as a Board we have taken steps to confirm our framework is appropriately calibrated to the relevant external market to support attracting and retaining exceptional executive talent. We also identified opportunities to enhance the transparency of how the framework is applied, and the Board’s approach to remuneration decisions, including consideration of risk. This focus on greater transparency has resulted in a new section on key remuneration matters to supplement this letter. Details can be found on pages 184–185. # Remuneration Committee considerations Remuneration increases for the CEO and other executive key management personnel • Maintaining competitive executive remuneration is important for attracting and retaining talent in a global market. • In determining remuneration increases, the People & Remuneration Committee (Committee) considers remuneration benchmarking information from ASX and offshore comparator groups, broader workforce context, incumbent and market relativity, executive capability and delivery of sustained performance. • No increases were awarded to any executive key management personnel (KMP) in the 2024 financial year, with modest increases provided over the last four years on a targeted basis (ranging from 0% to 5.1% 1). • External remuneration benchmarking conducted in the 2024 financial year review identified that FR for the CEO and other executive KMP was not competitively positioned relative to CBA’s size, scale and performance. Refer to pages 188–189 for more information. • While prior decisions by the Committee to deliver no or modest remuneration increases reflect a measured approach, mindful of shareholder perception over time, this does give rise to notable risks in our ability to retain our executives. • As a result, the Board decided to take action to address competitiveness for CBA’s ELT in the 2025 financial year in an increasingly competitive local and global market. Committee considerations Long-term alignment remuneration award (LTAR) • The LTAR was introduced in the 2021 financial year when the executive remuneration framework was redesigned to significantly reduce total remuneration opportunity (a reduction of up to 19%) and to increase the proportion of total remuneration deferred over longer time horizons (currently up to five years for GEs and six years for the CEO), in line with CPS 511. • The framework is compliant with CPS 511 which requires a material weighting to non-financial measures for variable remuneration. • Together the LTAR and LTVR support a collective focus on sustainable shareholder value creation, with the LTAR performance assessment considering consistent performance in leadership and strategic execution, reflecting long-term risk and performance outcomes. • The Board completes an annual pre-grant assessment to determine whether executive performance has met expectations or if performance warrants a reduction to the LTAR grant value. A pre-vest assessment was formally introduced in the 2023 financial year to further strengthen the focus on non-financial outcomes over the long term as a driver of sustainable shareholder value creation. • While the FY22 LTAR award does not formally require a pre-vest assessment, the Board conducted a look-back review over the four-year LTAR restriction period and determined that no adjustments were required and the FY22 LTAR vested in full. CBA’s executive remuneration framework is designed to attract and retain exceptional executive talent, align with and support sustainable shareholder returns, and meet regulatory requirements. The Board reviews the competitiveness of executive remuneration on an annual basis, taking into account role scope and scale, and incumbent capability and experience. Competitiveness is assessed via external benchmarking, primarily with consideration of other Australian peer banks (ANZ Group (ANZ), National Australia Bank (NAB) and Westpac Banking Corporation (WBC)) and large ASX listed companies, with supplementary consideration of remuneration in global jurisdictions, particularly where we have sourced or are at risk of losing executive talent. Our ELT has an average tenure of four years in a GE role, with valuable executive experience providing strong, stable leadership for the Bank. The team has a track record of delivering sustainable performance and significant value for shareholders, with TSR of 220% delivered over the past five years. In this context, maintaining competitive remuneration is critical to improve our ELT’s market position against both Australian and relevant offshore comparator groups. In Australia and offshore, we have observed competition for talent for various critical functions and in senior layers of management, including below executive KMP level. Despite anticipating increasing competition for talent, we have experienced some regrettable turnover to Australian peer banks. Following a comprehensive market review, the Board implemented a number of FR increases across the ELT during the 2025 financial year. These increases are designed to help improve competitiveness and our ability to retain the executive talent required to deliver our strategy and achieve continued high performance and long-term value creation. # Group Risk & Remuneration Review Committee CBA Board Group Risk & Remuneration Review Committee Management Committee that advises the Group CRO on risk considerations for determining remuneration outcomes for Executive Managers to Executive General Managers, including Specified Roles. Independent remuneration consultant The People & Remuneration Committee may engage external advisors to provide information to assist the Committee in making remuneration decisions. Board Committees Concurrent meetings are held to determine CEO and Group Executive risk, performance and remuneration outcomes. People & Remuneration Committee Oversees CBA’s remuneration framework and assists the Board to ensure the Group’s remuneration strategy, policies and practices are appropriate and eﬀective. Audit Committee Assesses and advises the People & Remuneration Committee of any audit matters which may impact collective and/or individual remuneration outcomes. Nominations Committee Considers and reviews matters relevant to evaluating the performance of the CEO and reports the evaluation to the People & Remuneration Committee and the Board. Risk & Compliance Committee Advises the People & Remuneration Committee of material risk matters which may impact collective and/or individual remuneration outcomes. People & Remuneration Committee and Board oversight The People & Remuneration Committee is the governing body for developing, monitoring and assessing the remuneration strategy and framework across CBA on behalf of the Board, ensuring that these are aligned to regulatory requirements, appropriate and operating as intended. The role of the People & Remuneration Committee is to review, challenge, assess and, as appropriate, endorse the recommendations made by management for Board approval. The Board reviews, challenges, applies judgement and, as appropriate, approves the People & Remuneration Committee’s recommendations. The People & Remuneration Committee met formally eight times during the 2025 financial year with the following members (as at 30 June 2025): Simon Moutter (Chair), Lyn Cobley, Paul O’Malley and Mary Padbury. The responsibilities of the People & Remuneration Committee are outlined in its Charter, which is reviewed annually. The Charter is available at commbank.com.au/peopleandremuneration As part of the performance and risk review, and to support the determination of remuneration outcomes for the CEO and Group Executives, the People & Remuneration Committee meets concurrently with the Risk & Compliance, Audit, and Nominations Committees. These concurrent meetings provide an opportunity for the Committees to review and recommend relevant risk and audit matters that may warrant consideration in the People & Remuneration Committee’s determination of remuneration outcomes. Information provided to the concurrent meetings supports the review and recommendation of collective and/or individual remuneration arrangements, including outcomes and variable remuneration adjustments. Considerations at the meeting include risk scorecard outcomes for the CEO and Group Executives, details of material risk matters presented by the Group CRO and outcomes of internal audit reviews conducted during the year, presented by the Group Auditor. The concurrent meeting process is structured to support the determination of appropriate remuneration outcomes and meet regulatory requirements. The meeting agenda primarily focuses on key risk and audit matters relevant to the CEO and each Group Executive’s performance and remuneration outcomes so that consideration is given to both exceptional and

The concurrent meeting process is structured to support the determination of appropriate remuneration outcomes and meet regulatory requirements. The meeting agenda primarily focuses on key risk and audit matters relevant to the CEO and each Group Executive’s performance and remuneration outcomes so that consideration is given to both exceptional and poor risk and audit outcomes and the context in which those outcomes occurred. The Group Risk & Remuneration Review Committee is a management committee that advises the Group CRO on risk considerations for determining remuneration outcomes. This Committee also reviews the application of remuneration consequences for poor risk behaviours and/or outcomes on accountable individuals from Executive Managers to Executive General Managers, including Specified Roles. In line with regulatory requirements, the performance and remuneration arrangements and outcomes of the CEO ASB are approved by the ASB Board and reported to the PRC with the request that the PRC recommend them to the CBA Board for approval, contingent on the ASB Board approval. External advisors During the 2025 financial year, external advisors were engaged to provide information to the People & Remuneration Committee to assist the Committee with making remuneration decisions. The People & Remuneration Committee did not seek or receive any remuneration recommendations from external advisors in the 2025 financial year. Executive remuneration framework in detail Fixed remuneration Fixed remuneration (FR) comprises base remuneration (i.e. cash salary) and superannuation (KiwiSaver for the CEO ASB). FR is delivered in accordance with contractual terms and conditions of employment and is reviewed annually against relevant comparator group remuneration benchmarks. As part of the benchmark, the Group’s size, scale and complexity relative to the comparator group are considered. Features Approach Purpose Varies remuneration outcomes in line with annual performance achievement, with material weighting to financial and non-financial outcomes across shareholder, customer, people and leadership and strategy execution measures, incorporating both risk scorecard and values assessments. Opportunity Target STVR: 75% of FR Maximum STVR: 94% of FR (125% of target STVR) Performance measures and weightings Individual STVR outcomes are determined on the basis of Group (or ASB for the CEO ASB) performance and individual performance through a balanced scorecard. Features Approach Purpose Varies remuneration outcomes in line with longer-term performance achievement, with a focus on relative shareholder returns to support sustainable shareholder value over time. Performance period Subject to relative TSR performance over four years from 1 July 2024 to 30 June 2028. Holding period • CEO: PRs that vest after performance testing (vested PRs) will be exercised into ordinary CBA shares, which remain subject to a further two-year holding period (to 30 June 2030). • Group Executives: vested PRs will be exercised into ordinary CBA shares, which remain subject to a further one-year holding period (to 30 June 2029). • CEO ASB: PRs remain subject to a further one-year holding period (to 30 June 2029). Performance measures and weightings • 50% measured against a general ASX peer group. • 50% measured against a financial services peer group. Instrument The LTVR award is granted as PRs. Remuneration report (continued) Performance measures Approach Relative TSR • Relative TSR provides a robust and easily quantifiable performance measure with strong alignment to shareholder value. • TSR measures share price movement, dividends paid and any return of capital over a specific period. • Relative TSR compares the ranking of CBA’s TSR over the performance period with the TSR of other companies in a peer group. Performance measure framework Under the LTVR, PRs are tested at year four and are subject to a further holding period. For the CEO and Group Executives, the PRs will vest and be exercised to ordinary CBA shares subject to the holding period. For the CEO ASB, the PRs will vest after the holding period has expired subject to vesting conditions. During the 2025 financial year, CBA’s consequence management processes identified 1,959 instances (FY24: 2,259) of substantiated misconduct, with 184 (FY24: 180) resulting in termination. Additional details on our approach to sustainability can be found on page 68. Risk assessment in performance and remuneration CBA’s performance and remuneration frameworks support effective risk management by holding employees individually and collectively accountable for managing role-related risks, encouraging behaviour that aligns with the Group’s values, performance management framework, and Code of Conduct. Employees are also required to complete Group mandatory learning. Group-wide risk assessment guidance including examples is regularly reviewed to set clear expectations of managing risks for both employees and managers, and to help people leaders consistently assess risk behaviours and outcomes, determine the appropriate level of STVR adjustments for not fully meeting expectations, and document the reasons for their assessment. ELT risk assessments continue to be supported by executive risk scorecards, independent assessment by the Group CRO, and the Board Committees meet concurrently as part of the interim and annual performance assessment processes. Comprehensive reporting is provided to the Board to support its oversight of risk assessment and remuneration outcomes and to inform the Board’s guidance for the annual performance and remuneration review.
