Scope – customer emissions In general, we calculate our financed emissions using estimates of customers’ Scope 1 and 2 emissions. 1 We consider the availability of Scope 3 data and methodologies on a sector-by-sector basis. 2 This year we have continued to include Scope 3 emissions for our thermal coal mining, upstream oil and gas extraction, and heavy industry portfolios, reflecting a relatively high coverage of customer-reported activity data or Scope 3 emissions across these sectors. Due to limited availability of customer-reported emissions we do not include Scope 3 emissions for some business lending sectors prescribed by PCAF for inclusion from 2023 onwards, such as other mining, other manufacturing and transport. We do not estimate Scope 3 emissions for commercial property and Australian housing due to limited available embodied carbon emissions data and methodologies. In aviation and shipping, it is common for customers to lease aircraft and vessels. The emissions associated with these aircraft and vessels would represent Scope 3 emissions for the customer. Where we identify such leases, for clarity of presentation and consistency with our sector-level financed emissions goal and target, we include the emissions associated with the aircraft or vessel in the customer’s Scope 1 and 2 emissions. For more information on Scope 3 measurement, see pages 402–403. In line with the PCAF Standard, when we refer to our financed emissions this is absolute gross emissions. Where data allows, we aim not to reflect our customers’ use of carbon credits, or customers’ avoided emissions or emissions removal. Where we use customer-reported emissions in our estimates, our efforts are largely dependent on the availability of gross reported emissions by third-party data providers, such as NGERS, Bloomberg and US EIA. Where we rely on estimation using emissions factors, we prioritise the use of gross emissions where available, such as Exiobase (extracted from the PCAF database) and Australian National Greenhouse Accounts. the use of gross emissions where available, such as Exiobase (extracted from the PCAF database) and Australian National Greenhouse Accounts. Due to the scale of our portfolio, we may not always be able to confirm that emissions data is presented on a gross basis, this may improve over time with the adoption of mandatory reporting standards. Limitations with diversified companies and data availability To estimate our financed emissions, we generally allocate each customer to a specific sector, using ANZSIC codes. Where emissions intensity multipliers are used, we calculate the emissions for that customer based on their allocated sector. Accordingly, if a customer is diversified across business activities, the estimate of their emissions may lead to an under- or overstatement of financed emissions at the sector level. Financed emissions calculations use point-in-time financial data and also use emissions data reflecting a 12-month period. There can be lags in customer emissions data which impacts alignment of timing with financial data. Financed emissions restatement policy Financed emissions methodologies and data continue to evolve. Sector-level financed emissions goal and target methodology This methodology is used for the sector-level goal and target graphs on pages 116–129 of the Strategy section. We take a sector-level approach to measure and track the alignment of our financed emissions with pathways to limiting global warming to 1.5°C. For sectors where we have set sector-level financed emissions goals or targets, we aim to measure customer emissions across a defined component of the sector scope that captures the most material emissions within the value chain, and set reduction goals and targets that are consistent with limiting global warming to 1.5°C, based on science. In order to achieve this, there are a series of additional methodological considerations for our sector-level financed emissions goals and targets. The table on page 405 summarises key choices. Defining the sector scope For each sector, this involves setting boundaries to define the emissions a customer is responsible for and collecting the required data to measure the emissions. We use ANZSIC codes as well as business knowledge to assign customers to the most appropriate part of the value chain. The table on page 405 defines the sector scope for each of our sector-level goals and targets. Selecting goal and target metrics In line with Net Zero Banking Alliance (NZBA) guidance, we set goals and targets using absolute emissions or physical intensity. However, we may choose to use other metrics, for example absolute financing, where relevant. We have found: • Absolute emissions goals or targets are most appropriate in sectors where science indicates the output has to be reduced substantially and, in some cases, completely by 2050 to limit global warming to 1.5°C. Data limitations may also support setting an interim goal or target based on absolute emissions, for example in the shipping sector. • Emissions intensity goals or targets are appropriate when the output in question may in fact grow, but at a decreasing emissions intensity. These intensity goals or targets should be based on physical metrics, for example kWh for power generation or m2 for housing. For emissions intensity goals or targets, an aggregation method is required to produce a portfolio metric. For power generation, heavy industry, aviation and road transport we use the attributed generation or production method. This approach divides the total attributed emissions by the total attributed activity. For Australian housing and Australian commercial property, we calculate a portfolio emissions intensity by dividing the total attributed emissions by the total attributed living area or floor area, respectively. Selecting reference scenarios When selecting reference scenarios, three criteria are important to us: 1. Consistent with limiting global warming to 1.5°C. 2. Providing geographical and sectoral relevance. We analyse various scenarios which are widely used by the industry. In May 2021, the International Energy Agency (IEA) published the Net Zero Emissions by 2050 scenario (NZE 2050) which shows a pathway for the global economy to achieve net zero emissions 20 years earlier than the previous Sustainable Development Scenario (SDS). We have selected the IEA NZE (2021), which is consistent with limiting global warming to 1.5°C, as our reference scenario for thermal coal mining, power generation, upstream oil and gas extraction, aviation and shipping. The NZBA identifies the IEA NZE (2021) as a scenario that meets the objectives of the NZBA commitment. A global 1.5°C-aligned reference scenario does not necessarily reflect Australia’s starting point or emissions trajectory. We track the portfolio emissions intensity against the IEA NZE (2021) however, we calculate the power generation target against the IEA SDS for OECD nations, based on total electricity and heat sectors CO2 emissions divided by total electricity generation. Our 2030 target of 105 kgCO2/MWh is 33% below the equivalent figure in the global IEA NZE (2021) scenario. We originally tracked towards this value based on the IEA SDS for OECD nations and chose to retain it as our 2030 target as it represents a lower emissions intensity than the IEA NZE (2021) transition pathway in 2030. Transport – Australian road (passenger and light commercial vehicle finance) The Australian road (passenger and light commercial vehicle) sector includes lending for the finance of passenger vehicles and light commercial vehicles. 1 Passenger vehicles include both cars and motorcycles. We have chosen a combined goal, recognising that many light commercial vehicles are used primarily as passenger vehicles and the decarbonisation profile is expected to be similar across these vehicle types. The goal metric is an intensity metric (gCO2/vehicle km) calculated by dividing the attributed Scope 1 emissions (gCO2) from motor vehicle finance (as described on page 397) by attributed distance travelled (vehicle km). Distance travelled currently reflects average distance travelled by vehicle type based on data published by BITRE. Attributed distance travelled reflects distance travelled multiplied by the attribution factor, where the attribution factor is the outstanding loan amount divided by the value of the security at origination. Where valuation data is unavailable, 100% attribution is assumed. Approach to climate scenario analysis Climate scenario analysis is a rapidly evolving field, with global scenarios regularly produced and updated. We use assumptions and inputs drawing from credible, global climate scenarios produced by the NGFS and obtain input from external experts when necessary. We review our choice of scenarios to check, in our view, they have plausible and appropriately severe outcomes; are consistent with legislative requirements and market practices, including use by peer banks; and they have appropriate sector and geographic data readily available. We use a combination of credible, long-term global climate scenarios that provide consistent inputs and assumptions for differing futures, as well as a range of acute scenarios to explore the impact of individual severe physical and transition events that could impact the Bank in any given year. This approach helps us to consider the changing impacts on the Bank’s financial prospects and risk profile over time, due to long-term chronic physical risks; increasingly frequent and severe acute physical risks; evolving transition risks arising from regulatory change, technological advancements and evolving stakeholder expectations; and opportunities that may arise to improve climate resilience and finance the transition. Depending on the nature of changes in the scenarios, in some cases, we may look to rerun previous analyses using updated information. Input used in climate scenario analysis Input/assumption Details Relevance to CBA’s assessment of our resilience to climate-related changes, developments or uncertainties • The Bank may be exposed to both physical and transition risks through the provision of deposit and lending services to retail, business and institutional customers. • The long-term scenarios are based on the NGFS scenarios which are

to CBA’s assessment of our resilience to climate-related changes, developments or uncertainties • The Bank may be exposed to both physical and transition risks through the provision of deposit and lending services to retail, business and institutional customers. • The long-term scenarios are based on the NGFS scenarios which are a set of climate-related scenarios designed to help financial institutions and policymakers assess the risks associated with climate change and the transition to a lower-carbon economy. They are therefore directly relevant for use in assessing the resilience of the Bank’s strategy and business model in the short, medium and long term, to the impacts of a changing climate. • Acute event scenarios were also run to consider severe but plausible climate-related events that could impact the profitability of the Bank in any given year. Diversity of scenarios • The long-term scenarios included a high transition risk scenario (Net zero 2050); higher transition risk scenario (Delayed transition) and a high physical risk scenario (Current policies) to enable the assessment of a range of plausible climate physical and transition risk outcomes and to address the uncertainty of potential developments associated with the trajectory of climate change. • The acute event scenarios assessed the impact of different acute physical climate events (cyclone and drought) and a transition event (NSW electricity disruption), on a diverse range of the Bank’s portfolios (retail, non-retail and agriculture). Climate-related physical or transition risks • The assessment of financial risk for each of the scenarios focused primarily on either the physical risks or transition risks relevant to that scenario. • For the strategic and non-financial risk types in the CRMA the scenario factored in both the transition and physical risks, where relevant or material. For example, under the physical risk scenario (Current policies) conduct risk may be heightened due to decisions the Bank may make in relation to pricing and lending practices in high physical risk zones. Under the high transition risk scenario (Delayed transition) conduct risk is also expected to be heightened for the same reasons in the short and medium term due to physical impacts from existing greenhouse gas in the atmosphere. Alignment to the latest international agreement on climate change • The Delayed transition and Net zero 2050 scenarios are aligned to the Paris Agreement’s overarching goal to hold the increase in the global average temperature to well-below 2°C above pre-industrial levels. Time horizons used • The long-term scenarios extend out to 2050, with the CRMA assessing risks at the following time horizons: – Current term (within the next 12 months). – Short term (~3 years) to align with the Bank’s strategic planning cycle. – Medium term (~10 years) to align with the timeframe of when the NGFS physical impacts begin to diverge for the low versus high warming futures. – Long term (~30 years) to align with the Bank’s home loan portfolio where home loans can be contractually agreed to for up to 30 years. • The acute event scenario time horizons vary by scenario

the NGFS physical impacts begin to diverge for the low versus high warming futures. – Long term (~30 years) to align with the Bank’s home loan portfolio where home loans can be contractually agreed to for up to 30 years. • The acute event scenario time horizons vary by scenario based on the time expected for the economic- and credit-related impacts to flow through to the Bank. Scenario modelling approach and key assumptions Long-term scenarios and CRMA Modelling approach • The Bank selected three NGFS scenarios (Net zero 2050, Delayed transition and Current policies) for long-term scenario analysis and engaged an economic advisory firm (Oxford Economics) to develop macroeconomic forecasts aligned to the NGFS scenarios using their proprietary models. Tailoring of these variables was performed at a national level, with more granular analysis performed for a selection of higher transition and physical risk exposed industries and regions to capture parts of the Bank’s portfolio which may not follow national-level trends. • Industry segments with more granular macroeconomic inputs were selected based on the portfolio exposure to physical and transition risks analysis (on page 144), and included: – Agriculture (dairy and livestock) – Air and road transport – Heavy industry – Non-renewable power generation – Coal mining – Petroleum product wholesaling and retailing – Upstream oil and gas exploration and production • Regional segments for more granular macroeconomic inputs were selected by considering materiality as well as portfolio exposure to physical and transition risk analysis. They are a composite of Greater Capital City Statistical Areas (GCCSAs) and Statistical Area Level 4s (SA4s): – Sydney – Rest of New South Wales – Melbourne – Rest of Victoria – South-East Queensland (Greater Brisbane, Gold Coast, Sunshine Coast and Toowoomba) – Rest of Queensland – Western Australia – Adelaide • The macroeconomic variables were then input to the Bank’s suite of stress testing models to arrive at balance sheet and credit loss results extending out to 2050. Scope of operations • Macroeconomic inputs associated with each long-term scenario were applied to all retail and non-retail portfolios of the Bank, including ASB. • The CRMA assessed the impacts of climate change on our financial, non-financial and strategic risk types. This included consideration of impacts on our business model, financial and non-financial risk, strategy, and climate-related risks and opportunities. Reporting period • The scenario analysis and CRMA were carried out during the last quarter of the 2025 reporting period. # Modelling Acute event scenarios – Key variables and assumptions Series of severe cyclones over South-East Queensland Modelling approach • An external actuarial consulting and analytics firm was engaged to model the paths of two severe (Category 4) cyclones making landfall in the South-East Queensland (QLD) region in consecutive years, providing estimated damages at a property level associated with wind, storm surge and cyclone induced flooding. • Each of these Category 4 cyclones is currently individually assessed as 1-in-200-year events, however the probability of two severe cyclone events in successive years in this location is currently extremely low. • Property-level damage and regional assumptions were run through the Bank’s home loans stress testing models to assess expected credit losses. • To model non-retail credit losses, the Bank’s industry subject matter experts considered the impact of damages and business disruption on the credit profile of industries with higher inherent risk of impact from floods and cyclones. Adjusted credit ratings were run through the Bank’s non-retail stress testing model to assess expected credit losses. Timeframe A five-year timeframe was selected to reflect the time expected for the economic and credit-related impacts to flow through to customers. Data as at The cut-off date for the data used for modelling was December 2024. Scope of operations • The retail scope of this scenario included CBA and Bankwest residential mortgages and Viridian Line of Credit (VLOC) accounts within the cyclone impacted regions in South-East QLD. • The non-retail scope focused on cyclone impacted regions across the following industries: commercial property; agriculture and forestry; mining oil and gas; manufacturing; transport and storage; business services; construction; wholesale trade and retail trade. Key inputs and assumptions • Damage from cyclone events – Damage ratios were modelled by an external provider and applied in year one and year two. The modelling considered a range of factors including distance from cyclone path, windspeed and topography. • Insurance coverage (retail) – The likelihood of insurance was modelled by an external provider. This data was complemented by underinsurance assumptions derived from research. • Insurance coverage (non-retail) – Overall insurance rate assumptions were internally developed and allocated using random sampling. • Insurability declines – Following each cyclone, insurance premiums were increased by ~20% and take-up rates were reduced. • Mortgage repayment stress – The ability of borrowers to make mortgage repayments was stressed through factoring in the extent to which costs for demolition, repair and alternate property rental during repair are covered by insurance, and the repair period. Customers were assumed to have defaulted where the costs to repair and sell the property exceeded the equity in the property, or where the customer was in negative equity. • Unemployment rates – A significant rise in unemployment rates was assumed to occur in the cyclone years with an increase of 8% and 20% from 2024 by the end of year two for Brisbane and regional South-East QLD, respectively. Unemployment improves from year three as infrastructure is repaired and jobs are created during the rebuild.

rise in unemployment rates was assumed to occur in the cyclone years with an increase of 8% and 20% from 2024 by the end of year two for Brisbane and regional South-East QLD, respectively. Unemployment improves from year three as infrastructure is repaired and jobs are created during the rebuild. • Residential building value declines – Aligned to damage ratios applied to each property. A linear return to pre-cyclone values over the repair period is assumed. • Residential land value declines – Varied by flood risk ratings for each property up to reductions of 35%. Key sources of scenario uncertainty and limitations There are a range of uncertainties when looking to model scenarios and their climate-related impacts. Understanding uncertainty within climate modelling allows us to focus on reducing it where possible, accepting it where necessary, and interpreting and communicating results in an appropriate manner. We consider the risks of relying on uncertain information when making decisions based on climate scenario analysis and we aim to avoid false precision in modelled outcomes, for example by rating physical risk across an entire portfolio rather than expecting single address results to be equally robust. There are limitations and uncertainties associated with projections of future climate scenarios, given

making decisions based on climate scenario analysis and we aim to avoid false precision in modelled outcomes, for example by rating physical risk across an entire portfolio rather than expecting single address results to be equally robust. There are limitations and uncertainties associated with projections of future climate scenarios, given the limitations of current scientific understanding of the climate system, its cascading impact to the broader economy and society, and complexity of climate risk modelling. The table below highlights a non-exhaustive list of some of the key sources of uncertainty and the range of limitations. Modelling area Key sources of uncertainty and limitations Long-term climate scenarios • Global climate models are highly complex and can be used to simulate possible future climates under various scenarios, such as different global warming trends. While they are grounded in physical principles and evaluated against past observations, their projections carry uncertainty due to the complexity of the climate system. • Economic variables for long-term scenarios are projected over a 25-year time horizon, with assumptions regarding factors such as policy and technology. There is considerable uncertainty over the pace and impact of climate change on the environment (physical risk) as well as how global and domestic governments will act to address it (transition risk). These projections could therefore be inaccurate. • Long-term scenarios do not attempt to predict the timing and extent of individual acute physical or transition events that could materially impact the Bank’s financial performance in any given year. Rather, the cumulative effect of such events is factored into macroeconomic variables used to model these trends. Although this approach enables a clearer view of any trends over time, it underestimates potential losses to the Bank because it does not account for localised declines, or direct impacts on asset values from severe climate physical or transition events that could occur in any given year. • Climate transition risk can materialise in a variety of ways including through direct exposure to carbon prices or indirect impacts from reduced demand. This creates significant difficulty in modelling or quantifying impacts. • The tailoring of the NGFS scenarios to the Australian context, at a national level and at a more granular level for higher transition and physical risk exposed industries and regions, was performed by the economic advisory firm (Oxford Economics) using their proprietary models. These global economic and industry models make assumptions about aspects such as trade, competitiveness, capital markets, interest rates and commodity prices, and may assume certain relationships observed in past data that may not continue under future climate conditions. Assumptions made about Australia’s specific conditions, including government policies, energy generation mix, geographic dispersion and general macroeconomic conditions may not be correct. • Long-term scenarios extending out to 2050 require balance sheet assumptions over the next 25 years. of these offsets, and express no conclusion about whether the offsets have resulted, or will result, in a reduction of 1,000 tonnes of CO₂-e.
